name: Afrikaans

ancestors.notes: Cape Malay substrate: some vocabulary; contact with Malay-speaking slaves

notes: Afrikaans (Standard Afrikaans). Descended from 17th-century Dutch of VOC settlers (Cape Colony, established 1652), but its sound system diverged far enough that a Dutch grapheme table is not a usable starting point. The table here follows Wissing's Illustration of the IPA (JIPA 50/1, 2020), which gives the inventory as eight short vowels /i y ɛ ɑ ə œ ɔ u/, four long /eː øː oː aː/ and three diphthongs /əi œy œu/. Points where Afrikaans differs from Dutch and where an inherited Dutch value would be wrong: ⟨w⟩ is /v/ (was /vɑs/) and ⟨v⟩ is /f/ (vas /fɑs/), with [ʋ] only an allophone of /v/ after /t k/ (twaalf, kwaad); short ⟨u⟩ is /œ/ (mus /mœs/ 'sparrow'), not Dutch /ʏ/; short ⟨i⟩ in a closed syllable is /ə/ (mis /məs/ 'mist'), with /i/ spelled ⟨ie⟩ (nies /nis/); the diphthongs are /əi/ (spelled ⟨y⟩ or ⟨ei⟩, byt /bəit/), /œy/ (⟨ui⟩, buit /bœyt/) and /œu/ (⟨ou⟩, bout /bœut/), not Dutch /ɛi œy ɔu/; and the long mid-high vowels /eː øː oː/ are phonetically diphthongal [iə yœ uə] (Wissing 2020, fn. 10, following Combrink & De Stadler 1987 and De Villiers & Ponelis 1987), so ⟨ee oo eu⟩ are transcribed here as those diphthongs rather than as monophthongs. NOTATION OF THE LOW VOWELS: two conventions are current. Wissing writes /ɑ/ short and /aː/ long, following the Dutch tradition; De Villiers & Ponelis (1987) and Coetzee (1981) write /a/ short and /ɑː/ long, and Wissing's own fn. 11 records the split. This spec uses the Afrikaans-internal convention (/a/ short, /ɑː/ long), which is also the convention of the wikipron gold scored here. The choice is notational: it does not assert a different vowel quality from Wissing's. CIRCUMFLEX VOWELS ⟨ê ô û î⟩ mark long lowered vowels (Donaldson 1993, ch. 1) and had no entries at all before; without them the letter was silently deleted and the rest of the word mis-segmented (môre → [mrɛ]). ⟨'n⟩, the indefinite article, is [ə] and is carried as a word exception; the apostrophe elsewhere marks elision and is silent. FINAL DEVOICING (Auslautsverhärtung, Wissing 2020: 132 — hoed /ɦud/ [ɦut], wind /vənd/ [vənt]) is declared here in positional_graphemes. It is NOT inherited from nl: positional_graphemes do not cross the parent link, so before this it simply did not apply and God surfaced as [xɔd]. GOLD CONVENTION DIVERGENCES, documented rather than fitted: the wikipron gold writes ⟨g⟩ as uvular [χ] (357 aligned mismatches, 2.8% of gold characters), while Wissing's consonant table places /x/ in the velar column and the uvular column holds only the trill /ʀ/; no fetched source supports the uvular fricative, so the spec keeps /x/ and pays the cost. The same gold writes the centring diphthongs with lax first elements [ɪə ʊə ɪø] where Wissing has [iə uə yœ] (a further ~300 mismatches). Substrate: Cape Malay vocabulary; Khoikhoi influence is mainly outside pronunciation (Wissing 2020: 127). VOWEL LENGTH BEFORE /r/: Afrikaans does not share Dutch's pre-/r/ lengthening of /i y/ — see NL_HIGH_TENSE_LENGTHENING_BEFORE_R_I's notes for the gold counts and the measurement. Dutch-only citations do not legislate for Afrikaans.

Afrikaans does NOT lengthen the tense high vowels before /r/, so the two rules inherited from nl (NL_HIGH_TENSE_LENGTHENING_BEFORE_R_I/_Y) are disabled here by re-declaring the ids with no phonemes. The Dutch rule is Booij 1995, ch. 2, a statement about DUTCH and not about its daughter; Afrikaans wikipron gold refutes it outright -- /i/ runs 24 [ir] to 4 [iːr] and /y/ 23 [yr] to 3 [yːr], i.e. 6:1 and 7.7:1 AGAINST lengthening, the mirror image of Dutch (2.0:1 and 2.9:1 FOR). Afrikaans has largely lost contrastive vowel length (Donaldson, *A Grammar of Afrikaans*, Mouton de Gruyter 1993, ch. 1). Measured on af wikipron against the current table: disabling them scores PER 0.1653, inheriting them 0.1695.
See NL_HIGH_TENSE_LENGTHENING_BEFORE_R_I above: same refutation by af gold (23 [yr] to 3 [yːr]), same disabling.

Disabled inherited Dutch rule: it targets lax /ɪ/, which Afrikaans does not have. Wissing 2020 gives the short front high vowel as /i/ (nies /nis/) and the closed-syllable ⟨i⟩ reading as /ə/ (mis /məs/), so there is no [ɪ] slot for the rule to rewrite.

stress.notes: Germanic word-initial stress on native vocabulary; Wissing 2020 records that Germanic prefixes and suffixes are normally unstressed and mostly have schwa as nucleus (JIPA 50/1: 137). Declared so that the unstressed-⟨e⟩ reduction in positional_graphemes has a stress assignment to key off; Wissing's final-syllable stress for monomorphemic and Classical-origin words is NOT modelled here (no sourced ending list to key it on).
